crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Cognitive rehabilitation covers therapies and supports for people with attention, memory, language, executive function, or social cognition difficulties after injury or illness. It spans stroke, traumatic brain injury, multiple sclerosis, dementia, and developmental conditions, and it is delivered by clinicians, therapists, and caregivers. In neuroinformatics, the field overlaps with brain imaging, electrophysiology, and digital biomarkers that help describe a person's cognitive profile. AI enters as a way to score tests, adapt task difficulty, and track change over time, not as a replacement for clinical judgement.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Cognitive rehabilitation systems run on data from neuropsychological tests, imaging such as MRI and EEG, wearable sensors, speech and language samples, and interaction logs from computer or tablet tasks. These streams are stored in clinical data systems, research databases, and sometimes personal devices, which raises questions about privacy and data quality. Models may run on local workstations, hospital servers, or cloud platforms, depending on the sensitivity of the data and the rules of the care setting. Real-time applications, such as adaptive training or brain-computer interfaces, need low latency and reliable hardware.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Clinicians and researchers define cognitive targets, collect baseline measures, and use AI to personalize task selection, difficulty, and feedback. Common approaches include supervised learning on labelled test scores, reinforcement learning for adaptive training, and natural language processing for speech and writing samples. Validation often compares model outputs with standard neuropsychological assessments and functional outcomes, and it may use cross-validation or external cohorts. The work is iterative, with human review of model suggestions and regular checks for bias across age, language, and education levels.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Cognitive data are sensitive, and they can reveal health status, disability, and sometimes identity, so consent, de-identification, and access control matter. Provenance includes where training data came from, who labelled it, and whether the model was validated on the population it will serve. Risks include misclassification, over-reliance on automated scores, privacy breaches, and unequal access if tools are not tested across languages and cultures. Regulation varies by country, and the site's 219 compliance and regulation pages reflect how quickly the rules are developing.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect more adaptive, multimodal systems that combine imaging, speech, and behaviour to tailor rehabilitation over months, not single sessions. Remote monitoring and digital therapeutics may extend therapy beyond the clinic, but they need evidence that gains transfer to daily life. Brain-computer interfaces and closed-loop stimulation are early, and they raise additional questions about safety, agency, and long-term effects. The field will likely move toward shared benchmarks, transparent reporting, and clearer pathways from research prototypes to clinical use.
